articles.title: Socialism Deferred: The Communist Party of Italy and the Historic Compromise of 1976
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: American politics is at a crossroads. All that was once considered certain or possible is now in question. For the first time since the early 20th century, American Socialists are gaining considerable municipal and state level influence through successful and highly publicized electoral campaigns. After a largely successful midterm showing, the DSA established itself as a small but potent force in American politics. For the first time there is a comparatively large cohort of elected DSA members holding local, state, and federal office. Along with this heightened political influence comes greater political risk. Questions of electoral positioning and maneuver take on greater weight. Examining the past experience of socialist and non-socialist alliances can be instructive. Italy provides a pertinent example of a large socialist party, the Italian Communist Party (PCI), that entered an election in 1976 that seemed to have it poised on the precipice of entering government for the first time since the onset of the cold war. This did not occur. Instead, it offers an example of the critical importance of electoral strategy, social research, and ideological flexibility. Despite a major electoral breakthrough with a historic 34% of the vote in 1976, the Italian Communist Party (PCI) was unable to translate this into a wider challenge to the institutional and economic order in Italy. The Communist Party benefitted from the leadership of Chairman Enrico Berlinguer, widely recognized as a particularly charismatic and talented politician. He and his associates pursued a strategic alliance with the Christian Democrats known as the Historic Compromise to bolster future electoral efforts. In reality the compromise undermined the long-term viability of the PCI project. Its failure stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of the mandate delivered by voters as well as a failure to anticipate the political realities of being a subordinate non-governing party to the Christian Democrats. At no point did the DC share power with the PCI. The party agreed initially to a non-sfiducia regime, meaning it promised not to call for a vote of no confidence. Ultimately, the PCI endorsed the government under long-serving and known conservative Christian Democratic Prime Minister Giuliio Andreotti in 1978 even though the party was denied any ministerial positions. Transitioning from the no-confidence regime to the “National Solidarity Government” the PCI still did not receive a meaningful stake in national power. Forced to defend unpopular measures, it ultimately entered the next election of 1979 in a worse position, presaging a process of decline throughout the 1980s and ultimate dissolution in 1991. the cold war dilemma of the pci The Italian Communist Party in 1976 was a mass based electoral Socialist Party confronted by the harsh political realities of the Cold War. It was viewed by many in the center and on the right as an agent of Moscow, functioning to subvert the democratic order. Simultaneously, to many Italian workers, peasants, and increasingly large shares of the petty bourgeoisie as well as students, the Italian Communist Party was a vehicle to advance democratic struggles that ranged from the armed resistance to Fascism to the right to divorce. Berlinguer and the leadership of the PCI correctly viewed their reliance on the Soviet Union as an obstacle to the democratic transfer of power. They formulated a new political line to demonstrate that the Party was a responsible democratic institution while also remaining faithful to the class struggle. Having its foundation in longserving leader of the Party and prominent Communist International Official, Palmiro Togliatti’s, recognition of Parliament as a legitimate vehicle for class struggle and his belief that there were multiple national roads to socialism, the line adopted by the PCI came to be known as “Eurocommunism” (a view adopted in different ways by the French, Spanish, and Italian Communist parties). Eurocommunism revolved around the idea that it was possible to utilize the parliament of bourgeois republics to peacefully transition from capitalism to socialism. This perspective tied all three parties (though the French would eventually break with Eurocommunism) to electoralism. This raises a basic problem: how does one retain the revolutionary goals and impetus of Socialism while supporting a bourgeois electoral process? The ideological basis of the Historic Compromise was established by Berlinguer in a series of articles released in the main party newspaper and official organ, Rinascita. Berlinguer was starting from a position of perennial opposition to not only the DC, but the entire spectrum of “bourgeois ideology”. To accomplish the ideological shift, he separated, in line with Italian historic experience, anti-Imperialism from absolute anticapitalism: “It is the duty of communists and all who fight for the cause of democratic progress and of the liberation of the people to raise the level of consciousness regarding these truths, in order to direct vigilant attention to all of the threats that imperialism and the ruling bourgeois class poses to the freedom of people and independence of nations.” (1) This opened the line of reasoning that would allow a Party militant or longtime supporter to consider that the cause of democratic progress writ large may constitute sufficient ideological similarity to the Communist commitment to anti-Fascism, thus to allow for the Communists to stand in alliance. This was not sufficient, however. To confront decades of inherited bias against accommodation with the DC, Berlinguer sought to employ one of the most potent symbols of the PCI, the Resistenza. Referencing the Salerno Turn when the Kingdom of Italy joined the Allies in World War Two through an agreement of all of the Anti-Fascist forces in the country, he wrote, “The more profound sense of the turn (at Salerno) was the necessity and the desire of the Communist Party to come to terms with all of Italian history, and with all of the historic forces (Socialists, Catholics, and others with democratic inspirations) who were present on the national scene and who fought alongside us for democracy, for national independence, and unity.” (2) By invoking the broad anti-fascist front of wartime, he was suggesting it might be reconstituted in the present. Berlinguer concluded, “If it is true that a democratic renewal can only be realized if it is supported by vast majority of the population, there is not only a need for a policy of large social alliances but also a determined system of political agreements that fosters a convergence and collaboration between all of democratic and popular forces until there is realized a political alliance among them.” (3) This justified the fundamental political logic of the historic compromise, that it was acceptable for the PCI to explore uniting with non-Communist forces to oppose Imperialism, that there were historic forces in the country (Socialism, Catholics, others) who could be united with today because of their role in the historic anti-fascist struggle, and that a revolutionary democratic program can only be pursued through a system of large social and political alliances. What Berlinguer did not anticipate was that the convergence he spoke of would lead voters toward the DC, not the PCI. the irony of the historic compromise Not only was the PCI suddenly forced to defend, in the name of the Historic Compromise, unpopular government policies such as the partial elimination of the scala mobile, rising costs of living due to inflationary monetary policy, and a partial dismantling of the gains earned by the unions during the previous round of labor militancy; it also faced internal dissatisfaction. There was widespread confusion among the Party: “From the start, much of the PCI membership was surprised and confused by the historic compromise; many were jolted when the leadership proposed an alliance with a political force that had been seen as the enemy for so long.” (4) According to Lucio Magri, author of the Tailor of Ulm and one of the founders of Manifesto, a leftwing journal that split from and ultimately rejoined the PCI, “If anything, younger and more combative sections of the population, less accustomed to discipline and delegation, wanted to participate in decision-making and to see the results sooner rather than later.” (5) This internal confusion was aggravated following the election because, “The PCI constituencies expected the party to use its leverage to push through far-reaching reforms. Instead the leadership devoted all its efforts to working out a formal agreement with the DC, backing down on major issues to keep negotiations going…the DC passed a series of measures that served its own interests…raising prices for the basic consumer goods, public transportation, and utilities; and dismantling the cost of living escalator mechanism (scala mobile), which protected the organized working class against inflation.” (6) Here were the perils of being a junior coalition partner. The PCI was not in government but because of the Historic Compromise was forced to defend policies that undermined its own position among its constituents in the name of a broader goal: namely, to demonstrate its “fitness” to govern. Even those elements within the Party that supported the Historic Compromise, according to Magri, were expecting reform but received only defence of the status quo, “Even those convinced of the rightness of Berlinguer’s project not only hoped for but willed a profound change in economic and social policy, and in Italy’s international position, mode of governance and distribution of power. A compromise maybe – but not subaltern cohabitation.” (7) the road not taken Was this the only path available to Berlinguer? Some both on the left and among disinterested historians saw another potential avenue that could have been pursued but was not explored; a Left Unity Coalition between the PCI and the Italian Socialist Party (PSI) – and smaller Left parties. An effective electoral coalition depended both on ideological unity and a program focused on the desires of the PCI base; namely, defense of the scala mobile and living standards of the popular classes, and an end to the corruption identified as a by-product of DC rule. Both the PCI and the official newspaper of the Italian Socialist Party, Avanti, regularly called out the corruption of the DC. The prospective coalition would also have entailed a defense of NATO, but with a varied foreign policy that at times would have been at odds with the NATO’a wider positions, for example, leaning on traditionally good relations between Italy and the Arab Republics. (8) Historian Paul Ginsborg notes that “…the country was crying out for change and reform. It would not be possible to achieve either by making an alliance with the DC. Berlinguer, it is argued, should have capitalized upon the enduring movement of protest in civil society in order to forge an alternative to Christian Democrat politics entirely.” (9) The PCI could not have taken power immediately, but it could have used the years after 1976 to build a united opposition, and to prepare the terrain for a decisive victory at the next elections.” (10) This suggests a qualitatively different view of the potential for the democratic transition in a bourgeois republic. While it was not realistic for a Left Coalition to assume power in 1976, the process of unity coalition building could have served as a vehicle for the consolidation of the Left into a more viable alternative pole in Italian politics. Nor did the PSI represent the only available alliance partner. There was as well the New Left which existed in various forms, ultimately to be joined by the explosive mixture of new social actors and popular demands that emerged on the scene with the Movement of ‘77. the italian new left To the Left of the PCI was a nebulous group organized around a handful of prominent thinkers such as Mario Tronti, Antonio Negri, and Silvia Federici. While their positions can be considered generally Left, they varied significantly on who or what constituted the proletarian class or revolutionary subject. Loosely, they agreed upon a broad conception of politics that placed the organization of the working class as something to be pursued outside of the boundaries of established organizations such as existing trade unions and the Communist or Socialist Parties. For this reason they adopted “Autonomia” (Autonomy) as the label for a body of wide ranging Marxist thought. Alongside this creative application of Marxism were numerous other ideological projects that embraced a variety of ideologies and identities; together they occupied a nebulous space best defined as the “New Left”. While there were numerous periodicals and journals such as Potere Operaio, Primo Maggio, Quaderni Rossi, etc. that all expressed different currents of thought to the left of the PCI, we can view the New Left coalition party, Proletarian Democracy (DP) as the primary organization in question, at least with regards to electoral matters. In the 1976 election the party received approximately 550,000 votes which earned it 6 Members of Parliament. (11) While not decisive, they represented a viable left-wing ally that when taken together with the Socialists at 9% would have allowed for the emergence of a Left Coalition in Parliament that the DC would have had to accommodate in some fashion, even as broader ideological unity was explored. The PCI’s refusal to engage with the New Left could be understood as a combination of old sectarianism and a fundamental misunderstanding or inability to recognize the new insurgent populations that defined the New Left. It is no coincidence that only several months later, after the elections, the Movement of ‘77 exploded onto the scene of Italian politics, expressing many different tendencies and modes of thought, but overall frustration with the existing political status quo, including the PCI. Magri summarizes the composition of the Movement of ‘77: “It was mainly a protest movement in a period of general downturn, mostly driven by anger and disappointment, and kindling huge hopes for a new world…its social base was new and heterogeneous: various marginal groups (unemployed youth, rank and file union activists in the railway and health sectors, jobless graduates), clustered together, or tried to cluster, around the students, whereas industrial workers were neither much in evidence nor the class centrally at issue in the protests.” (12) Clearly, this heterogeneous movement was far from being composed of the PCI’s traditional base, that is the industrial working class. But it represented exactly the constituency for a broader Left alliance against the Center and Right. It could be seen then that the failure of the PCI to extend a meaningful hand to the New Left for the Election of 1976 was a profound error. The Party’s aversion to ideological compromise, its unwillingness to cede ideological and organizational control of the coalition, was fatal. Of course, it also reflected the Party’s opportunism in seeking to secure a grand alliance with the DC. the politics of the possible Was the Left Unity Coalition realistic? The experience of the prodigal Manifesto group which had split from the PCI in the 1960s to form an independent Marxist journal and returned by the late 1970s and the Proletarian Unity Party for Communism which experienced a similar trajectory, both demonstrate that small ideologically left dissident factions were able to dissolve and return to the PCI proper. This suggests a degree of underlying compatibility. Ironically the PCI by refusing to pursue a meaningful alliance with the wider forces of the left contradicted Togliatti’s own thoughts regarding parliament, “In the second place, it is necessary for the parties that fight for socialism, and the communist parties in the front rank of them, to be strong, numerous, well organised and for them to know how to work and fight in such a way as to win a decisive influence in the decisive strata of the working class and the people. In the third place, it is necessary for these parties to be united in their action, because this not only increases their numerical weight…but can allow them to establish a reciprocal understanding and a collaboration with those political forces that are not hostile to social reforms of a socialist type and to a consequent policy of peace.” (13) Furthermore, had the PCI been basing their perception of the role of parliament in 1976 on the broad call for democratic unity advanced by Togliatti – following the logic of the Historic Compromise itself – the unity of the PCI, PSI, DP, and Italian Social Democratic Party (PSDI) could have been pursued under the wide umbrella of anti-imperialism and in defense of democratic values. There also existed a degree of popular support for this position, reported in Avanti.. A press conference of neighborhood leaders appearing in the Party’s official organ indicated that there also was a degree of PSI support for a broader understanding of the left. (14) The Socialist leadership around De Martino could have been approached by the PCI to draft a new unity program to create an alternative center-left coalition. Martino himself advanced a lukewarm but open position at the PSI party congress of 1976, stating in his address to the Party that it was critical that the PSI consider a left-wing alternative politics and observed that some elements within the Party were insisting that the PSI declare they would not join any government without the PCI. (15) While retaining a desire for autonomy and flexibility going into the election, De Martino recognized that the primary strategic goal of the PSI was, “to build a leftwing alliance and alternative.” The failure of the PCI then is not that it rejected an immediate electoral alternative based on alliance with the PSI, but that it did not, after the election, devote energy to constructing a long-term autonomous left alliance that could in time replace the DC. The difficulties in synthesizing a Left Unity Coalition among the PCI, PSI, New Left, and Others were significant. They represented notable differences in viewpoints regarding many issues. However, given the growing popular dissatisfaction with the DC, historic inter-party relations particularly between the PCI and PSI was not impossible. Ginsborg highlights that, while difficult, the decision to not pursue a Left-Unity Coalition would have fateful consequences as, “In the summer of 1976 the opportunity, albeit fraught with difficulty, existed for building an alternative to the Christian Democrats. The opportunity was not taken, and no such chance was to present itself again. the italian lesson What does the Italian General Election of 1976 teach us about the potential rise of Socialist Governance in the United States in the wake of the 2026 Midterm Elections? The 2026 Midterms are not the Italian General Election in 1976. Unlike the PCI which was a well organized, disciplined, national political force, the DSA is still a pre-party formation employing primarily democratic electoral infrastructure to contest specific races. While the PCI could rely upon professional cadre to coordinate national efforts, the DSA is composed primarily of volunteers. Like the General Elections in 1976 Italy, the DSA has made a tremendous breakthrough, relatively speaking, with six candidates being elected to federal office and numerous downballot or endorsed victories. (16) Despite this success, the DSA remains fundamentally subordinate to the Democratic Party. Because of the need to oppose the Republican Party and the still relatively marginal position of the Socialist Movement in the USA, the DSA like the PCI, is compelled to support policy packages pushed by the Democrats that are fundamentally antithetical to a Socialist vision for the United States. But the DSA may suffer should their bourgeois partners, who constitute the actual power in government, pursue policies that undermine the DSA. To combat the effect of being tied to a larger bourgeois force, the DSA must expand its political imagination which the PCI refused to do. It is imperative that socialists seize the mandate offered by voters and propose meaningful reforms to meet immediate material expectations. Simultaneously, it is possible to begin an ideological process of Left Coalition Building which may mean that while a still marginal force in 2026, the DSA enters 2028 and beyond as an independent political party capable of advancing the socialist project and vision that motivates its membership. To speak of coalition building is also to highlight the stark difference between the possibilities open to the PCI that do not exist in the same measure for DSA. Unfortunately, there are no comparably sized overtly Socialist parties that the DSA can join hands with to create the beginning of a coalition. That said, there are options the DSA can cultivate. Third parties such as the Greens, Working Families Party, and others who are not explicitly Socialist could unite with the DSA in a Popular Democratic Coalition; or at least on specific initiatives like the Green New Deal or Cost of Living, that might prepare the ground for later and broader convergence. Similarly there is the possibility of establishing an explicitly political alliance with progressive and independent elements of organized labor. This would be distinct from the broad imperative of supporting the unions as vehicles for securing tangible gains for working people and would represent an effort to create a specific political project transitioning from solely economic initiatives towards broader related challenges. Progressive Democrats are seemingly a potential coalition partner but represent an acute danger for the DSA. They are exactly the mechanism by which the DSA can be maneuvered into supporting candidates and policies that undermine the position of the DSA which could include continued support for Zionism, continued “legal” deportations, or continued funding for foreign wars. That said, Progressive Democrats could be persuaded to provide indirect material support for the DSA by channeling funds and resources to DSA initiatives. This does not amount to joining a formal Popular Democratic Coalition, but nonetheless could help. The common thread running through all of these options is the necessity for the Popular Democratic Coalition to have a specific end goal in mind. Unity for the sake of unity was not viable nor beneficial for the PCI nor would it be viable for the DSA. articles.title: David Dinkins Wasn’t Loud Enough for New York City
articles.author: David Duhalde
articles.content: In the past few weeks, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed breaking up the Strategic Response Group and closing Rikers by 2032 , the former established by progressive Mayor Bill de Blasio, who also revived a plan to dismantle the latter by 2027. But unfulfilled promises of police and carceral reform efforts go back to the 1990s. How much should the failures of previous mayoral administrations weigh on the decisions of Mamdani and his allies in regard to public safety and police? This question has no easy answer. But a new book by James Barney on the tenure of New York City’s first black mayor, David Dinkins, offers insights on his efforts to rein in police excesses based on new research, especially in the local press of the era — and critically how those attempts failed, despite Mayor Dinkins’s desires and promises. In A Fragile Alliance: David Dinkins, Coalition Politics, and the Struggle to Govern a City in Crisis , Barney, while sympathetic to Dinkins, argues that both Dinkins’s quiet leadership style and inability to create a narrative uniting his own multiracial coalition, much less the majority of the city, proved to be his undoing, dooming his reelection prospects and much of his agenda. Barney, critical of identity politics throughout his history book, sums up his reservations here: . . . in particular, Dinkins’s reliance on the mosaic metaphor betrayed a worldview that privileged difference. While Dinkins repeatedly noted that New York City was a “gorgeous mosaic,” in a “mosaic” each of the pieces is different. They only produce any meaning by being part of a larger piece of art. But this type of thinking was at the heart of Dinkins’s problems as a leader because it emphasized differences rather than commonalities. Barney’s reservations about celebrating difference are at times too determinative. For instance, I doubt Dinkins could have done much to stop the disintegration of the New Deal/Great Society coalition that voted Democratic as white ethnics left the party across the country. But Barney’s concerns about the communication failures of Dinkins’s tenure were real and went beyond narrative to style. While noble at times, the mayor’s quiet leadership style prevented New Yorkers — especially in a time without social media to get news rapidly and easily outside major media like Mamdani enjoys and uses today — from seeing their mayor’s interventions that created more peace than was seen elsewhere in America at the time, for example Los Angeles, which experienced a much deadlier upheaval triggered by the lack of convictions for the police who senselessly beat Rodney King, as well as the killing of teenager Latasha Harlins by a Korean American storeowner. This failure provided an opening to power for demagogues such as Rudy Giuliani to paint a darker picture around crime and disorder than actually existed. While New York City’s political landscape has changed in many ways — the Staten Island secession movement, for example, is almost forgotten today — one thing Barney covers remains very much the same. The New York Police Department (NYPD) and institutions around it enjoy strong independence from civilian control that makes it difficult for any mayor to shape policy and personnel decisions commensurate with other major city agencies. A famous instance of this was when the Sergeants Benevolent Association (SBA) tweeted out personal data of then-Mayor de Blasio’s daughter’s arrest related to the George Floyd uprising. Former SBA head Ed Mullins eventually faced disciplinary charges over this, though by then it was overshadowed by his federal indictment and conviction of stealing from his members. It is difficult to think of any other agency and its unions who would feel so emboldened to reject democratic oversight. Dinkins, unlike most of today’s socialists and progressives, ran on a tough-on-crime agenda. He promised to hire thousands more police officers. The issue of crime polled high across racial and gender categories of voters. But Dinkins targeted his law-and-order proposals to include increasing policing in communities of color with officers of similar backgrounds. A major critic of this policy was Giuliani, who claimed this public safety policy would take police away from white neighborhoods. Giuliani’s racialized law-and-order rhetoric helped sink Dinkins. Progressive mayors following Dinkins, such as de Blasio and Mamdani, have reckoned with the political reality that a public safety reform agenda is territory that isn’t worth attempting battle upon. And losing puts their whole left-wing agenda, not just public safety, at risk. Case in point: after Dinkins’s defeat, New York saw two decades of fiscal conservative and anti-police-reform mayors. Crown Heights as a Turning Point Two chapters of the book that expand on how such demagoguery on policing helped cost Dinkins his mayoralty focus on the Crown Heights riots and Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association (PBA) riots, respectively. These chapters also go beyond those two episodes of public violence to discuss how other instances of excessive police force neither led to uprisings nor successful efforts to advance civilian control of law enforcement. Barney’s research uses these events to help us understand how perceived disorder would be viewed as a key reason Dinkins lost, even though the crime rates were falling, and how his relationship with the police leadership and rank and file did not recover despite his own law-and-order narrative. Dinkins won a surprise primary victory against three-term incumbent and bombastic erstwhile liberal Ed Koch in 1989. Barney credits Dinkins’s win through efforts to build a black-led, multiracial coalition out of the efforts in and around Jesse Jackson’s 1988 presidential campaign and subsequent Rainbow Coalition. Voter registration and mobilization, especially of black voters, to back Jackson were then used to elect Dinkins. Those new voters proved fruitful for Dinkins’s own Rainbow Coalition. Dinkins won over half the vote in the multicandidate Democratic primary against Koch. But his candidacy against the Republican in the general was unusually closer. In New York, the Democratic Party primary more often than not is the de facto election. Not for Dinkins. He faced Giuliani, famous at the time for his federal prosecution of the mafia in New York’s Southern District, in 1989 and 1993. Each time, the victor only bested his opponent by around 2 points. Not only were the margins similar, but Barney argues that themes in each election centered around crime, racial tension, and divisive ethnic politics. What made the difference was how a slim number of voters (turnout was roughly the same, 1.9 million in both mayoral races) eventually shifted toward a harsher response to perceptions of disorder, even as crime rates were declining. Dinkins lost ground partly because of both the Crown Heights riot and PBA riot. Each contributed to the public perception of an ineffective Dinkins, which undermined his promises to create a safer city and less brutal policing methods. The Crown Heights riot story officially begins on August 19, 1991, when a vehicle in a motorcade following the chief Lubavitcher (a sect of Jewish Hasidim) rabbi hit two Guyanese American children. The immediate lack of medical attention for the children by emergency medial technicians, explained by the Jewish volunteer service that initially responded to the accident lacking professional skills needed to treat the young people’s injuries, led to a retaliatory stabbing of a rabbinical student days later. The following unrest, in which 150 people were arrested and one hundred police injured, led the media to publicly question Dinkins’s ability to heal the racial and ethnic divide in the city and portray him as a weak leader. Footage of the 1991 Crown Heights riot in Brooklyn, New York. (Wall Street Journal Opinion / YouTube) But the conflict in Crown Heights went further back than these two incidents. The riot itself reflected the tension between the religious Jewish enclave and their black neighbors, largely of West Indian descent. In a city where fights over resources can feel zero-sum, the well-organized and self-isolating Lubavitcher community appeared to gain at others’ expense. Their leadership, politically well-connected as a result of their well-organized followers voting as a bloc, primarily looked after their own. Barney notes, for example, that the police protection for the Lubavitcher headquarters was seen as taking officers away from the crack epidemic, fostering further estrangement from their black gentile neighbors. Dinkins, viewing this as a battle of “good and evil,” according to Barney, responded to the restive state of Crown Heights by sending in a thousand police officers to quell the violence. Black civil rights leaders and organizers such as the Reverend Al Sharpton and Sonny Carson, at times previously allied with the mayor, turned on him. Sharpton even characterized Dinkins’s action as setting up an “apartheid state.” But a second, seemingly contradictory viewpoint sprung up from Giuliani and his allies that Dinkins actually held the police back from acting. This narrative fit well with voters that Barney says wanted to lump Dinkins, Carson, and Sharpton together. Dinkins couldn’t win. To make things worse, Dinkins publicly stated — repeating doctors’ misdiagnosis — that the stabbed rabbinical student would recover. But his wounds were fatal. The Jewish man died a few hours after Dinkins’s remarks. The death made Dinkins look, even if unfairly, incompetent. Barney credits much of the success the mayor did achieve in facilitating conservations between different Crown Heights faith leaders. These dialogues between Christian and Jewish leaders were rarely reported in the press. To Barney, this was just another example of Dinkins’s “quiet leadership” that, while noble, undermined public perception of governance. Ultimately, a 1993 internal city investigation called the Girgenti Report vindicated Dinkins from the viewpoint that he had not, in fact, held back the police nor abetted the prosecution of the rabbinical student’s killing. But the report’s timing was poor for the incumbent. Barney concludes it did more to remind voters in an election year of the chaos of two years earlier than absolving Dinkins in their eyes: “For a mayor who longed to unify, Crown Heights became the moment when broad segments of the public lost confidence in Dinkins and when his vision of a gorgeous mosaic, while laudable, was found insufficient to meet New York City’s realities.” The narrative that Dinkins held the NYPD back in Crown Heights was one of many that undermined his relationship with the police department and its officers. Another was that the overwhelming white police force felt the mayor was giving preferential treatment to people of color and criminals. The Police Riot as a Point of No Return In 1992, a police officer shot a Dominican immigrant in Washington Heights, which sparked a series of events that led to a police riot by September. The Washington Heights shooting seemed to be heading toward similar unrest — this time, sparked by young people who felt overpoliced. Dinkins was able to de-escalate the situation well, such that even his critics like Cardinal John O’Connor gave the mayor credit for his handling of the shooting’s aftermath. The mayor’s initial success and efforts included allies he recruited. Dinkins had an ally in Lee P. Brown, an African American criminologist and former police chief of Houston, Texas, that took the same role under Dinkins. As commissioner, Brown supported community policing, which brought more officers who looked like the people of the neighborhoods they patrolled. Again, this policy was not favored by some white people who felt it took resources from their residential areas. But this balance between reform and political reality in policing became unstable for both Dinkins’s coalition and the NYPD brass. At the time, the police practiced stop and frisk, an invasive and violating search practice that nearly exclusively targeted young men of color. Dinkins would come to regret this policy. Beyond the ethics, stop and frisk also fostered a schism in his coalition between the young people who felt brutalized and the older residents who wanted more police. Roscoe C. Brown Jr, a Tuskegee airman veteran quoted by Barney, summed up this division in the simple fact that black people had been victims of both crime and racist policing. Solving one requires tackling the other. But doing so for Dinkins became impossible. Brown resigned as commissioner in 1992, because, according to Barney, even this reformer did not want to go as far as Dinkins in empowering the police watchdog city agency, the Civil Complaint Review Board. Dinkins, unlike Brown, determined the NYPD was unable to hold itself accountable. Still, Brown’s departure was from the worst rebuke Dinkins would experience by the NYPD. A banner seen at the 1992 Patrolemen’s Benevolent Association Riot reads, “Dinkins, you sold out the NYPD.” (NY1 / YouTube) On September 16, 1992, organized by the police union (PBA), nearly ten thousand off-duty officers rallied outside city hall. Fueled by alcohol and rhetoric from Giuliani and PBA union leaders saying Dinkins favored criminals over cops, some police wore anti-Dinkins shirts, and others overturned barricades. While the media and some allies like Sharpton returned to Dinkins’s camp after this because of the racist slurs hurled at Dinkins and noxious nature of the police riot, the damage was done with enough of the public. The perception that Dinkins had lost the police overrode the actual declining crime rates with a sufficient number of voters to eventually swing the election toward Giuliani the next year. This would end a progressive holding the mayor’s office until 2014 with the election of Bill de Blasio. NYPD Reform Returns Today not only is the mayor a progressive but, like Dinkins, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Zohran Mamdani also shares the challenges of balancing the wishes of his coalition and campaign promises with those of political reality. Policing is no different. Recently, Mamdani has pledged to disband the Special Response Group (SRG), a controversial police unit with both counterterrorism and protest control duties, and also backed socialist councilmember Chi Ossé’s CURB Act, which would limit tactics employed by SRG. As the SRG’s responsibilities will be reassigned to other police units, a move reportedly supported by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, limiting existing practices that police reform advocates say they are most against is critical to the success of reform. Unlike Commissioner Lee with Dinkins, Tisch was not the incumbent mayor’s appointment but a holdover from the previous mayor. Mamdani has resisted calls from parts of his coalition to fire her; these allies identify her support of Zionism and a strong carceral state as incompatible with a socialist vision. Except for not hiring nearly six hundred more police officers after pushback from NYC-DSA and others, the recent moves against SRG nearly a year into his term are a first real push to tackle unaccountable and abusive police power. While New York City crime stands at record lows , the experience of Dinkins should serve as a warning that statistical realities such as declining rates are sometimes no match for scare tactics. The police still have soft and unchecked power, with council allies allegedly quietly opposing the CURB Act. Hidden opposition can become public, and allies can return. But sometimes it is too late, as Dinkins experienced after the police riot. As the title of Barney’s book reminds us, holding power can be fragile. It will take a balance of principle and strategic planning to successfully rein in the police. Or else we will set back again. A lesson the current mayor can also learn from Dinkins is in a communication style to avoid. Instead, he should continue to present an accessible vision and visible actions so voters and other members of the public can easily understand and repeat his policy priorities. Had Dinkins been able to enjoy the social media platforms and fluency that Mamdani does to get around mainstream gatekeepers and parochial local press, he might have been able to overcome the idea he was ineffective. But even with such tools, it requires a willingness to be public, even boastful, which people adverse to demagoguery understandably avoid. But good intentions can be fatal. Quiet leadership, while noble, may be silent even to your supporters. And it can be used against you by your enemies. The base needs to know what you’re doing to counter the inevitable lies and distortions thrown at left-wing politicians by their reactionary political opponents. The success of a progressive and socialist public safety agenda depends on winning the majority. That requires a tremendous amount of organizing from the grassroots, but also political leaders who can help echo a narrative that can cut through the noise trying to maintain the status quo or reserve the gains made by reformers so far. A Fragile Alliance is worth reading for anyone trying to comprehend how the past can weigh on today’s New York. It is a valuable resource in seeing how old attack frames, especially around identity, which seem outdated but once worked against Dinkins, could return against Mamdani. But more critically, how previous efforts of mayors around police reform failed and succeeded. Learning from that history can better prepare activists to push those in power, even our allied electeds, in a more strategic direction. articles.title: Wage Crisis
articles.author: Sonali Kolhatkar
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. With a new crop of Democratic senators and representatives heading to Congress in January, many are calling for their first order of business to be raising the federal minimum wage . Even Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is vying for the position of House Speaker and is known for being cautious , says raising the minimum wage is imperative . An Associated Press survey of voters in November 2026 showed that “About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a ‘crucial’ or ‘major’ factor in their vote for Congress.” Saru Jayaraman, the co-founder and president of One Fair Wage who represents 14 million restaurant workers, says Democrats have a “mandate” to improve affordability — but argues that politicians should focus more on raising wages than lowering prices. “While the cost of living can be brought under control, it can’t really fall,” she explains. “It’s not going to happen, nor would economists really suggest that it’s a good thing to happen. It’s called deflation.” Instead, she concludes, “We have to bring the pay up to the cost of living.” The federal minimum wage stands at a shockingly low $7.25 an hour and hasn’t been raised for nearly two decades. Many states have raised their own wage floors since then, but minimum wage workers in at least 20 states are stuck at this poverty level . Related: America's Billionaires Don't Donate to Politicians. They Invest in Them. Raising it should be step one for lawmakers elected on a wave of concerns about affordability. The MIT Living Wage calculator offers concrete guidelines for the wages people need in order to survive. Jayaraman points out that “the least you need to live anywhere in the United States right now, including the cheapest county in the U.S., which is McLennan County, Texas, is $25 an hour if you have even one dependent.” This past April, Reps. Delia C. Ramirez (D-IL), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-IL), Lateefah Simon (D-CA), and Analilia Mejia (D-NJ) introduced the Living Wage for all Act , raising the wage floor to $25 an hour nationwide. The act currently has 35 co-sponsors, while the Senate version of the bill has 4 co-sponsors. While $25 may sound like a large jump from $7.25, the increase is phased in over six years, and Jayaraman sees it as “a very slow and reasonable pathway to get closer to the cost of living.” The standard opposition to raising wages is that it leads to job losses . But there is plenty of evidence to the contrary. In states like California and New York , economists found that low-wage workers saw higher wages and more jobs after the states raised their minimum wages to $15 an hour, more than double the federal minimum. “When working people earn more, they spend it,” says Jayaraman, which in turn creates more jobs. “It doesn’t go to the Cayman Islands or a Swiss bank account like it would when we cut taxes for the wealthy. Instead, when you put more money in people’s pockets… they are spending it in the economy to survive, and therefore the economy does better.” In an exit poll of 10,000 midterm voters from around the nation, nearly 90 percent of people felt that raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour was somewhat, very, or one of the most important issues for them. The idea is so popular, in fact, that last year some MAGA supporters were circulating a viral social post falsely claiming that Trump had signed an executive order to raise the wage floor to $25. (Unfortunately, he didn’t.) Still, there is an expectation that President Trump will veto all Congressional legislation in 2027 to ensure Democrats can’t claim any wins. But Jayaraman urges Congress to pass it anyway. If the president does veto the wage hike, the opposition party can use it to their benefit in the next campaign. And if he signs it, everyone wins. OtherWords

articles.title: Inflation Is About Resources — and Power
articles.author: Oskar Brandt
articles.content: After prices began rising and rising in the wake of COVID-19 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, some blamed welfare and public spending for the inflation. Yet in many economies, weak demand and falling public investment after 2008 held back investment and productive capacity. Austerity can also weaken productivity and future growth. In the United States, changes to trade policy during Donald Trump’s first presidency added to uncertainty about the economic situation. Trade policy uncertainty between 2017 and 2018 may have lowered investment by 1 to 2 percent. During the pandemic, automakers canceled orders and halted production. Demand returned before factories, suppliers, and transport networks could restart. The Cleveland Fed documented how factory shutdowns, parts shortages, and shipping delays during the pandemic disrupted supply chains. The oil crisis of 1973 is a reminder of how a real supply shock can also become a lasting case for austerity. Joe Biden’s American Rescue Plan expanded the child tax credit. Child poverty fell from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, then rose to 12.4 percent in 2022 after Congress let the expansion expire. From 2019 to 2023, low-wage workers’ real pay grew by 13.2 percent. Real manufacturing-construction spending rose by 85 percent from January 2021 to a six-decade high in part as a result of new investment laws. These gains helped poor families, workers, and industry, though they cannot all be attributed to Biden’s policies. US inflation also fell earlier than in the eurozone. Consumer price index (CPI) inflation peaked at 9.1 percent in June 2022 and fell to 3 percent by June 2023, while eurozone inflation was still 5.5 percent . Global supply pressures eased, energy prices fell, and the Federal Reserve raised rates sharply. Still, stronger wages and public investment can coincide with falling inflation. The gains for poor families, however, can disappear when that policy ends. Sweden brings the question into focus in 2026. In its March 2026 forecast , the Swedish Agency for Financial and Public Management projected a general government deficit of SEK180 billion for the year. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) describes the fiscal policy as expansionary but expects headline inflation to remain below target. Inflation can rise when spending meets shortages of labor or natural resources, limited production, or firms with the power to raise prices. But spending and higher purchasing power do not cause inflation by themselves. The result depends on resources, production, prices, and import dependence. The deficit forecast and the IMF’s outlook show why. Production Is Power Imagine a low-paid worker with rent due and a child to feed two weeks until payday. A pay raise may help, but it cannot create affordable homes or medicine. When the costs of essentials rise faster than incomes, people with little room in their budgets absorb the shock first. Inflation policy decides who loses purchasing power, whose costs get protected, and whose prices remain beyond public control. A government that issues its own floating currency creates money as it spends and withdraws money from the private economy through taxes. But it still faces real limits: labor, technology, materials, energy, and ecological capacity. Reliance on imports, foreign-currency debt, and exchange rate pressure can tighten those limits. If spending exceeds what producers can supply, prices may rise. A deficit alone cannot tell us where that point lies. An economy with available workers and room to raise productivity can absorb spending without necessarily generating inflation. Banks create money when they lend . Each loan creates a matching deposit; as the loan is repaid, that deposit money disappears. But money cannot summon nurses, electricity, medicines, homes, or skilled workers. Private credit can sustain demand when wages and public spending lag, but households and firms cannot increase debt indefinitely. When borrowers repay loans more quickly than banks issue new ones, this bank-created money contracts. Austerity can exacerbate this fall in demand. If households and businesses try to pay down debt at the same time, a financial crisis can ensue. Globalization gave rich countries access to abundant goods and helped keep some prices down, but it tied factories to long shipping routes and distant suppliers. Military power can protect routes, resources, and property rights, but it also depends on domestic industrial capacity and state support for its industries. Japan, South Korea, and China built technical capacity through public investment, industrial policy, directed credit, protection, and managed trade, while many Western economies have become dependent on finance, services, and imported goods. This has weakened the West’s ability to sustain the military power that keeps globalization in place. Globalization also exposed the costs of weakening domestic industry. Trade shocks left factory workers with lasting job losses and lower incomes. Research has linked layoffs to far-right support , unequal exposure to economic shocks to racial animus and right-wing voting in the United States, and local trade shocks to authoritarian values . A company that dominates its market sector can raise prices with less fear of losing customers. Across industries in fifteen European economies, the average market share of the four largest firms rose from 26 percent in 2000 to 32 percent in 2019; average markups rose about 7 percent. A US manufacturing study found that mergers were associated with higher markups and little evidence of higher plant productivity. Firms can also use monopsony power to hold down wages and hiring. In a study of French labor markets, a 10 percent increase in labor market concentration was associated with nearly 0.9 percent lower wages for new hires and 12.4 percent fewer hires. Shocks Give Price-Setters Cover COVID caused real supply problems . Lockdowns disrupted production. Households saved more, while spending shifted from services to goods. Auto demand plummeted in 2020, causing carmakers to cut their chip orders. In turn, chipmakers shifted production to other customers, and when auto demand returned, they could not quickly meet carmakers’ renewed need. Shortages can make it easier for powerful firms to raise prices. When rivals face the same shock and customers expect increases, price hikes can spread even without a cartel. In 2022, profits rose faster than production across the eurozone and accounted for the largest share of price increases. Real cost shocks, like those associated with the recent US wars of 2025–26, can nonetheless coexist with wider margins. In food markets, financial speculation and stockpiling can drive price rises beyond what shortages alone would explain, especially when war creates expectations of shortages. When COVID arrived, manufacturers expected a prolonged recession and cut production, capacity, and orders. Demand and employment recovered faster than expected, leaving shortages of semiconductors, lumber, and other inputs. Fiscal expansion did not invent these bottlenecks; it revealed them. Repeated periods of weak demand can close factories, disperse skilled workers, and delay investment, making supply slower to recover. In the 1960s, large industrial firms had built capacity but struggled to sell everything they produced. Some responded by buying unrelated businesses, selling off or outsourcing production, and relying more on short-term finance. This shift away from production gave financial markets greater influence over industrial decisions. In the decades that followed, private debt could temporarily sustain productive capacity despite weak wage growth, but when borrowing slowed, spending and sales fell. Debt-led crises also enabled investors to buy distressed property, companies, and assets from poor households cheaply, at a high social cost. Debt and Austerity Some Mesopotamian rulers in antiquity periodically canceled debts , freed people from debt bondage, and restored property, in part to check mass indebtedness and land concentration. These measures were episodic, not part of a regular, universal system. Debt was contested in Ancient Greece too, as seen in Solon’s reforms . Rome faced recurring credit crises and public-land conflict . Debt crises and land struggles shaped the politics of the late Roman Republic. The two world wars showed that markets could be governed. During World War I, the US War Industries Board coordinated production. After the war, advocates of austerity in Britain and Italy promoted balanced budgets and hard-money policies and accepted high unemployment as ways to restore economic hierarchies at labor’s expense. During World War II, the United States used price ceilings, rationing, taxes, wage policies, credit controls, and resource allocation to restrain inflation, raise revenue, and direct production toward the war effort. One historical estimate put the price level more than 30 percent below where it would have been without general price controls. Controls did not abolish scarcity. Many goods were rationed or simply unavailable, but alongside public management of demand and physical resources, the controls worked. World War II was one of the few times that the US came close to full productive capacity. During the war, labor shortages and stronger unions also improved many workers’ bargaining position . A study of 166 elections in 16 OECD countries from 1980 to 2016 found austerity associated with increased electoral abstention and support for nonmainstream parties. Austerity weakens workers’ bargaining power and public services, reduces demand and investment, and can undermine social stability. The late 1990s surpluses, combined with the trade deficit, pushed the US private sector into record deficits. Household debt grew much faster than income as Washington paid down public debt . Levy researchers later linked private sector deficits to the global crisis of 2008. Post-COVID inflation had different causes, including supply bottlenecks , a shift toward goods, and energy shocks. Lessons From Past Shocks Inflation was already rising in the United States before the 1973 oil shock. The US chose to escalate the Vietnam War . The war diverted workers, fuel, and materials from civilian production and sent dollars abroad. In 1971, Richard Nixon ended the dollar’s convertibility into gold. The dollar continued to serve as a major world currency without a promise of redemption in gold. Fiat money still faces real limits: the availability of oil, labor, materials, and productive capacity. During the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil states imposed an embargo and cut production . Separately, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) raised prices. Iran’s shah, a US ally, pushed for higher oil revenues to finance the country’s military buildup. Nixon had promised to sell him the arms he wanted. A contemporary account argued that Washington encouraged Middle Eastern producers to raise prices from 1971; Washington had earlier accommodated the shah’s push for higher prices, but during the crisis it opposed the Arab embargo and resisted OPEC’s proposed 100 percent price hike. The United States did not create the whole crisis. But US leaders accepted higher oil revenues for a strategic ally. Meanwhile, oil companies, banks, and arms firms gained from the new flows of money, while workers and households paid higher prices. Leaders later used the crisis to attack welfare and full employment, even though the oil shock did not prove that public spending caused inflation. The shift toward policies that tolerated high unemployment, wage restraint, and public spending cuts was a political choice, not an automatic result of the oil shock. Naomi Klein has traced disaster capitalism to Milton Friedman’s argument that crises can open the way for sweeping economic change. She shows how leaders and businesses have used this approach repeatedly, from Chile and post-Soviet Russia to the Iraq occupation and Hurricane Katrina, to push privatization and expand corporate control. This selfsame policy choice — the choice between using inflation to justify austerity, or addressing its causes and effects — is reflected in Sweden’s response to the latest energy shock. The Swedish Case The war in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz this past year, raising Swedish motor fuel prices by 25 percent. Yet Eurostat’s November release put Swedish inflation at just 0.6 percent, compared with 4 percent in the eurozone. On the Riksbank’s target measure , which holds mortgage interest rates fixed, Swedish inflation rose from 0.7 percent in August to 1.5 percent in September before easing to 1.1 percent in October. Excluding energy, it was just 0.1 percent in October. Some measures that widened Sweden’s deficit also lowered prices. The November budget projected a 2026 deficit of SEK158 billion, or 2.3 percent of GDP. After Sweden halved the value-added tax (VAT) on groceries in April, food prices fell 5.5 percent that month; a government review found that retailers passed on most of the cut. The government also subsidized half-price monthly transit passes from July through December. The Riksbank estimates that without the temporary measures’ direct effects on prices, September inflation would have been 3.0 percent, twice the actual rate. Growth continued alongside low inflation. Real GDP grew 1.6 percent, and the European Commission raised its forecast for 2026 growth to 2.8 percent . Household spending, investment, and net exports also lifted growth. The available figures give no separate estimate of how much the relief measures added to output or productivity. The labor market recovery has been slower. A labor force survey put trend unemployment at 8.7 percent in the third quarter, even as employment rose. Sweden has also cut support for people in employment programs for more than 300 days. The government expects the cuts to speed up the return to work. But when households on tight budgets cut their spending , local businesses lose sales; and if financial pressure pushes people into jobs that make poor use of their skills, productivity could suffer. Sweden’s 2026 figures do not yet tell us how large these effects are. The Riksbank expects inflation to exceed 2 percent in 2027 as the recovery strengthens and higher energy and import costs feed through. The government forecasts 2.8 percent in 2028 when the grocery VAT is due to return to 12 percent. Further disruption in Hormuz, the war in Ukraine, and new trade barriers could also raise costs and weaken demand for Swedish exports. Sweden can issue kronor, but what it can buy depends on the fuel, labor, and equipment available. Higher interest rates can slow spending and hiring, but they won’t bring another tanker through Hormuz. Cheaper fares leave commuters with more money in their pockets today, and better public transport gives them a way to use less imported fuel tomorrow. A state cannot buy resources that do not exist. But concentrated firms may raise prices before resources run out, while austerity can destroy demand and productive capacity. Inflation reflects pressure on real resources, but power determines who controls them and who pays when prices rise. articles.title: Under Capitalism, Socialism Will Never Disappear
articles.author: Alex McCarron
articles.content: If socialists and progressives had a good night on November 3, it wasn’t so much because they brought new ideas to the election, but because it was a chance to relitigate fights the Right thought it had won years ago: universal health care, Palestinian solidarity, and the expansion of the labor movement. We even got a rematch between George W. Bush–era Islamophobia and two of the Muslim Americans who had to live in its shadow, Adam Hamawy and Abdul El-Sayed. Many have lauded Zohran Mamdani’s novel use of the term “affordability” for the recent shift in political common sense. But while his branding is new, his politics are not. Mamdani has never styled himself as a new kind of politician. He seems to be constantly locating himself in history, comparing himself to Milwaukee’s sewer socialists and New Dealers like Fiorello La Guardia. This makes sense when you consider that his policies represent decades of struggle: the project of expanding democracy into the workplace dates to the late nineteenth century, and the fight to guarantee health care as a right dates to the early twentieth. Critics often ask why socialists are bringing a nineteenth-century ideology to bear on twenty-first century problems. The simple answer is that it seems to be what’s working. Since the turn of the twenty-first century, a series of global social movements have sought a new kind of political orientation, one that would allow for a break with the politics of the last century and the historical culs-de-sac they crashed into. Every few years brings a new form of right, center, and left politics: Occupy, Abundance, the Yellow Vests, the Movement of Squares, prison abolitionism. These movements all respond to real problems, but what’s new about them is mostly just branding. Few offer genuinely new critiques or build lasting political constituencies or institutions. Their strength is being novel enough to draw a crowd, drive a news cycle, or launch an academic career. Such innovations move to the same rhythm as capitalism’s own churning drive to simulate invention, revolution, and disruption across the economy. At the same time, one sees the appeal. We can’t exactly blame radicals for wanting a disruption of their current institutions. Everywhere you look, leftists are trying to overcome the NGOization of the Left and searching for a common ground between their alienated, specialized critiques. Ecologists want to talk about the environmental catastrophe of the genocide in Gaza, while anti-racists want to connect their work to the extreme weather events that disproportionally effect the Global South. This is the basic drive of left-wing politics: to establish continuities between spheres of knowledge and to build connections between people. The 20th Century Never Died To find that meeting place in socialism is to recognize that what is happening to you has been happening to you for a very long time. Embracing the old language means realizing that you’re settling unfinished business rather than facing a new foe. Comparing the capitalist class to the aristocracy that came before it enables a person to see how arbitrary and contingent ruling-class power really is. One can understand why Bernie Sanders traded loaded terms like “bourgeoisie” and “proletariat” for the “1 percent” and “99 percent.” But it was just as important that he held onto “democratic socialism.” The term signaled that he was continuing a struggle and adding to an existing tradition of critique rather than declaring a year zero for left politics. We are likely to be haunted for years by how dynamic, inventive, and exciting the twentieth century was. Every decade brought a new way of dressing, a new style of painting, and new stage in the maturation of cinema and popular music. Our hunger for political novelty is not just a reflection of market forces. It’s also a long shadow of that era of continuous revolution in politics and culture. Look closely, though, and you’ll find many of the twentieth-century movements that sought a break with tradition did so while grabbing hold of another tradition buried even deeper in history. Le Corbusier claimed his form of architecture would clear “the charnel house of past ages” that our homes had become, but he did so by marrying the mathematical proportions of the Parthenon to the logic of mass production. As much as Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso wanted to carry Paul Cézanne’s project into the future, they were also looking for a way to reconnect Western painting to the animism of African sculpture. The French New Wave paid an equally backhanded compliment to the “naive” genre films of Americans like Raoul Walsh and Sam Fuller, whose primitivism could liberate French filmmakers from their own pretensions and refinement. As Long as There’s Capitalism, There Will Be Socialists Even Karl Marx had this moment of paradox. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte , he writes that “the social revolution of the nineteenth century cannot take its poetry from the past but only from the future.” A few lines later, he quotes the Gospel of Luke 9:60: “Let the dead bury their dead.” Marx was inveighing against the tendency of revolutionaries to reach for the words and costumes of past eras when faced with the task of changing the world: Rome for the French Revolution, the Old Testament for the English Civil War. This awkward LARPing is what turns history’s repetitions into farce. Yet Marx’s famous line about history occurring “first as tragedy, the second time as farce” is itself framed as an amendment to Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. Even the poetry of the future has a few allusions in it. The difference between the French revolutionaries’ idealized Rome and today’s democratic socialism is that socialism is no more a thing of the past than capitalism is. Capitalism constantly calls the concept back into existence, raising its own gravediggers out of the grave, over and over again. As long as capitalism exists, it will exploit workers and destroy the planet, and the masses will find a way to fight back. Our present sits on a much longer timeline than the twenty-four-hour news cycle has accustomed us to. One day we’ll have new words and new costumes, but those belong to a new world, and we’re not there yet.
