articles.title: Anwar Shaikh Renewed Marx’s Economic Theory for Our Time
articles.author: Riccardo Bellofiore
articles.content: Anwar Shaikh, who died on October 6, 2026, was one of the most original economists of the last half-century. Few did as much to rescue the Marxian critique of political economy from its theoretical difficulties and develop it into a rigorous, empirically grounded analysis of contemporary capitalism. Shaikh’s ambition was extraordinary. He reconstructed classical political economy as an alternative to the neoclassical mainstream, understanding capitalism not as a system tending toward harmonious equilibrium but as a turbulent social order whose normal functioning generates competition, conflict, structural change, and crisis. I owe Anwar an immense intellectual debt . For more than fifty years, his writings were a source of inspiration and critical engagement. While our perspectives were never identical, his influence was deeply rooted in my thinking. When Marx Was Supposed to Be Dead I first encountered Anwar’s writings in the mid-1970s. In Italy, where I had studied with Claudio Napoleoni and wrote my dissertation on Rosa Luxemburg, the debate centered on Karl Marx’s theory of value and Piero Sraffa’s criticism of neoclassical economics. The demonstration that prices of production could be determined independently of labor values seemed to many economists to render Marx’s theory redundant. Others retreated into a primarily philosophical defense of Marx, preserving the critique of alienation and fetishism while abandoning much of its economic explanatory content. Anwar refused this alternative. In the 1970s and early ’80s, his writings were decisive in restoring Marx as a scientific analyst of capitalism. His contributions on the transformation problem, technological change, international trade, competition, and crisis challenged both the claim that Marx had been superseded by Sraffa and the tendency to reconstruct Marxian political economy using categories borrowed from orthodoxy. His celebrated 1974 article, “The Humbug Production Function,” exposed how apparently impressive empirical results could arise from algebraic identities rather than the neoclassical theory they supposedly confirmed. Mathematics, Anwar insisted, could not substitute for an explanation of the social relations underlying economic phenomena. His two articles on foreign trade challenged David Ricardo’s understanding of comparative advantage, demonstrating that international competition could reproduce persistent inequalities between nations without requiring monopoly or imperfect competition. His intervention in the transformation controversy showed that Marx’s procedure could be interpreted as the first step in an iterative process leading to prices of production. The essential issue was not simply mathematical consistency. Marx was investigating the historically specific relations of capitalist production, the exploitation of workers, and the processes through which accumulation transforms itself. What mattered was to recover and develop this distinctive object of inquiry. Anwar’s essays on Maurice Dobb and on the history of crisis theories, both published in 1978, were equally important. He showed that capitalist crises were not accidental departures from equilibrium, because they belonged to the system’s normal movement. To understand capitalist reproduction was simultaneously to understand its interruptions. For a generation that had witnessed the collapse of the postwar boom, these arguments were more than academic interventions. They restored confidence that Marxian theory could develop as a living research program rather than survive as a defensive orthodoxy. The Turbulence of Capital Anwar’s reconstruction of real competition was perhaps his most enduring theoretical contribution. From this perspective, competition was neither the harmonious mechanism imagined by neoclassical economics nor something abolished by the concentration of capital. It was a relentless struggle among capitals for profitability and survival. As part of this struggle, firms introduced machinery to reduce costs, undercut competitors, and obtain temporary advantages. Successful innovations spread, transforming productive conditions and undermining the advantages that initially motivated them. Decisions that were rational for individual capitalists could have contradictory consequences for capital as a whole. Mechanization, driven by the pursuit of extra profits, could contribute to a declining general rate of profit. As Vivek Chibber has reminded us, this view of competition also posed a challenge to the influential monopoly capital tradition associated with Paul Baran and Paul Sweezy. Anwar argued that its claim that concentration had superseded competition rested, paradoxically, on accepting the neoclassical identification of competition with perfect competition. This conception was central to my own interpretation of Luxemburg. In my dissertation, completed in 1976, I had explored how technological change emerged from both the antagonism between capital and labor within production and competition among capitals for extra surplus value. These processes could generate problems of realization and insufficient investment, without supporting a theory of capitalism’s inevitable collapse. Anwar gave me indispensable analytical tools for developing these insights. Probably, my subsequent reading of his work was more Schumpeterian than he would have accepted. I saw capitalist innovation as a dynamic of endogenous structural transformation that repeatedly displaced existing productive configurations. Anwar was more skeptical of Joseph Schumpeter, whose account he considered insufficiently emancipated from equilibrium thinking. My 1985 article on Schumpeter’s monetary theory of development and my 1989 essay, “A Monetary Labor Theory of Value,” developed this difference further. My intellectual formation owed much to Napoleoni as well as Augusto Graziani, Meghnad Desai, and Duncan Foley. For me, Marx’s theory of value was a theory of exploitation within the monetary circuit of capital, not primarily a theory of relative prices. I distinguished labor-power from living labor, arriving at the category of living labor-power: the capacity to work inseparable from the human beings who bear it. Its actual expenditure as living labor depends on capitalist command, cooperation, conflict, and resistance. Capital cannot purchase a predetermined quantity of living labor as an ordinary commodity. The extraction of surplus labor is contested; new value originates in this process and acquires its social expression in money. Anwar understood exploitation and capitalist command, but our approaches diverged over the connection between labor, value, prices, and money. The difference was especially over money. Anwar’s account of real competition and prices of production retained the classical notion of moving centers of gravity and treated money primarily in relation to exchange, prices, and profitability. I drew instead on Schumpeter’s bank-created purchasing power, Graziani’s monetary circuit, and Hyman Minsky’s financing of an uncertain future. For me, money is constitutive of capitalist production from the outset: bank finance gives firms command over labor-power before production begins, while sales subsequently validate the value produced. Money as initial finance is not merely money as universal equivalent, nor is financing production identical to financing investment. This did not make Anwar indifferent to credit or finance; it marked a different theoretical starting point. Different Crises of Different Capitalisms Our views of capitalist crises were different, but also complementary. Anwar’s distinctive contribution was his theory of profitability crises. Capitalist accumulation, he argued, follows recurrent long rhythms, in which phases of expansion eventually give way to prolonged downturns. Beneath shorter business cycles lies the movement of profitability, shaped by real competition, capital-intensive technical change, and the struggle over wages and working conditions. Particular historical shocks operate within these longer movements. For Anwar, the crucial incentive to accumulation was the rate of profit-of-enterprise, the difference between the general rate of profit and the interest rate. This distinction was central to his interpretation of the Great Recession, which he called the first great depression of the twenty-first century. The financial collapse of 2007–8 was the trigger, not the underlying cause. But he did not argue that the general rate of profit had simply continued to fall throughout the neoliberal era. On the contrary, he insisted that the attack on labor from the 1980s onward had restrained the decline in profitability, while the dramatic fall in interest rates had raised net profitability and sustained a substantial economic expansion. Against this backdrop, cheap credit simultaneously encouraged growing indebtedness and financial speculation. The recovery after the end of the postwar boom in the 1970s was real, but the conditions sustaining it could not be prolonged indefinitely. In his mature reconstruction, Anwar distinguished the normal maximum rate of profit, persistently eroded by capital-intensive technical change, from the normal rate of profit, whose decline could be counteracted by a rising profit share. His account of the neoliberal boom thus gave an essential place to countertendencies, without relinquishing the underlying logic of profitability-driven accumulation. I read Marx’s falling rate of profit as a metatheory of crisis, not a law generating identical outcomes in every period. Countertendencies can prevail yet generate new contradictions: rising exploitation may sustain profitability while aggravating realization problems, and struggles over living labor can challenge capitalist command directly. My reconstruction suggested a further historical distinction: the nineteenth-century Long Depression and the crisis of the 1970s were both crises of profitability, though arising from different mechanisms; the Great Crash of 1929 and the Great Recession beginning in 2007 revealed instead how the conditions sustaining capitalist expansion could generate crises of realization and financial breakdown. Anwar recognized the distinctive historical forms of these crises but sought their underlying unity primarily in the recurrent movements of profitability and accumulation. The crisis of the 1970s was for me not merely a wage squeeze but a crisis of the capital-labor relation itself: a difficulty in extracting the quantity and quality of living labor required by capital. The subsequent neoliberal restructuring transformed both production and finance, developing what I called privatized Keynesianism, sustained by asset inflation, private indebtedness, and politically managed monetary policy. Finance did not simply conceal the contradictions of a stagnant capitalism. It helped sustain accumulation and reorganize the conditions under which labor was employed and exploited. These were not arguments against Anwar’s theory of competition and profitability. They were attempts to develop a complementary account of how capitalist contradictions take different historical forms. Anwar engaged seriously with effective demand, credit, and debt, especially in his writings on Marx, John Maynard Keynes, and Michał Kalecki. Our disagreement was not about profitability versus demand but about how monetary finance, class struggle, and accumulation should be connected in a critique of changing capitalist forms. An Expanding Critique of Political Economy Over time, Anwar’s project expanded from the reconstruction and defense of Marxian political economy into an ambitious alternative framework grounded in classical political economy. Marx remained central, but the wider constellation included Adam Smith, Ricardo, Keynes, Sraffa, Roy Harrod, and Joan Robinson. In an autobiographical essay published in 2014, Anwar explicitly characterized his approach to growth as following a “classical-Keynesian-Robinsonian path.” This broadening of his intellectual horizons did not mean abandoning Marx, still less weakening his criticism of capitalism. It expressed his conviction that the classical tradition could provide the foundations for a modern science of capitalist society. Empirical investigation had been integral to Anwar’s work from the beginning. With E. Ahmet Tonak , he developed a Marxian reconstruction of national income accounts, distinguishing productive and unproductive activities and challenging the seemingly neutral categories of conventional statistics. His research on exchange rates, international inequalities, value-price relations, and profitability similarly connected theoretical arguments with systematic investigation of economic reality. Anwar participated in the international conference I organized at Bergamo in 1994, marking the centenary of Friedrich Engels’s publication of the third volume of Capital . His contribution, subsequently published in a volume I edited, Marxian Economics: A Reappraisal , investigated the empirical strength of the labor theory of value, drawing also on the work of Luigi L. Pasinetti. It illustrated a crucial aspect of his intellectual trajectory: Marx’s theory was not merely to be rescued through conceptual reconstruction. Its explanatory propositions had to confront empirical evidence. His association with the Levy Economics Institute, beginning in 1990, further enlarged his research. He engaged with macroeconomic modeling and with approaches related to Wynne Godley’s work without abandoning his classical foundations. All this culminated in his monumental Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises , a synthesis of decades of research. Few economists have attempted anything comparable. Anwar brought together competition, prices, wages, profitability, investment, effective demand, finance, international trade, and crisis into an integrated alternative to mainstream economic theory. Capitalism as he understood it was regulated through turbulence, not by the imaginary perfection of equilibrium markets. His intellectual curiosity remained undiminished: his later research ranged from international trade and exchange rates to econophysics, income distributions, and the measurement of inequality. Perhaps We Are Closer Than We Appear We met again at a conference in İzmir in October 2014 devoted to the causes of the global crisis. Our discussion returned to a question that had accompanied us for decades: How could Marx’s critique of political economy be developed to account for the transformations of capitalism, drawing on Keynes, Kalecki, and Minsky without losing its theoretical foundations? On this occasion, Anwar argued that our differences concerned primarily the movement from abstract categories to concrete capitalist reality. Marx had left his theoretical project unfinished, and subsequent economists had chosen different points at which to depart from it. Money, effective demand, and financial instability required further theoretical development but could not simply be added to Marx from outside. Anwar suggested that Keynes, Kalecki, and Minsky could be integrated into an account of accumulation driven by profitability, provided their contributions were critically transformed. He then concluded: “Perhaps we’re much closer than we appear to be.” I replied that I agreed with him word for word. My project was not an eclectic combination of Marx and later economists. At the beginning of my presentation, I had insisted on a distinction fundamental to my understanding of Marx: critique is not mere criticism. Marx did not simply reject Ricardo’s political economy as false. He appropriated its scientific insights, exposed their limitations, and transformed them within a different theoretical framework. The same task confronted us in engaging with subsequent theories and the changing realities of capitalism. This may also explain why, in his later work, Anwar became increasingly comfortable with a classical-Keynesian characterization of his theoretical project. An Unfinished Conversation Anwar’s intellectual independence was inseparable from his political commitments. He belonged to a generation for whom radical political economy emerged from struggles against war, racism, imperialism, and capitalist exploitation. He rejected both the false neutrality of mainstream economics and the reduction of critical theory to political slogans. As E. Ahmet Tonak has movingly recalled, he was also an extraordinary teacher. My MA students in Bergamo organized a reading group on his book, concluding with a video discussion with Anwar. He explained that a theory of capitalism could not emerge merely by adjusting orthodox assumptions: it required different questions and foundations. His generosity extended beyond academic life. I remember spending New Year’s Eve with him in 2017, shortly before a difficult period in my life. Our friendship mattered no less than our theoretical projects. We continued to exchange ideas in later years. In 2021, we discussed Sraffa, Marx, and money at considerable length, defending different interpretations while remaining attentive to each other’s arguments. At the conclusion of one exchange, Anwar wrote: “No doubt there are other issues on which we differ, but the mutual respect and affection remains. I raise a glass to our meeting again under better conditions.” Unfortunately, it will never happen. To me, Anwar’s legacy is not a closed theoretical system. It is an extraordinary example of how the criticism of capitalism can combine scientific rigor, historical understanding, empirical research, intellectual independence, and political commitment. For those of us who encountered his work in the 1970s, he helped make it possible to remain faithful to Marx without treating Marxism as an orthodoxy. For younger generations, he demonstrated that an alternative political economy could be developed rather than merely proclaimed. I will miss his friendship, his intellectual generosity, and his determination to pursue an idea wherever it led. Our intellectual dialogue will continue, at least in my mind. After more than fifty years of reading his work, I can think of no better way of honoring his memory. articles.title: Confederacy of Dunces
articles.author: Chuck Yates
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 1706, over three centuries before the start of the second Trump regime, Jonathan Swift wrote, “When a true genius appears in the world, you may know him by this sign, that the dunces are all in confederacy against him.” Swift had a good eye for the absurd, and knew a dunce when he saw one, but what would he think if he could see us now, with the dunces in charge and not a single genius anywhere in sight? At least two things seem clear. First, despite what his loyal followers think, Trump has proven that he’s no genius. He may have some knack for working a room, but so does any stand-up comic worthy of the name. It doesn’t take a genius to rouse a rabble. All you have to do is keep reminding people what they’re unhappy about, what they’re afraid of, and who their enemies are. It doesn’t matter what you say. If you just keep saying it every chance you get, it isn’t long before people start believing it, and in no time you’ll be fooling all of the people all of the time. And second, though many of Trump’s most faithful supporters may be honorable men and women, there also are plenty of dunces among them. Captivated by his promise to rid the country of rats, they’ve trailed along behind him like a gaggle of enchanted children following the Pied Piper. Will they continue to follow him, though, after the chaos he’s unleashed in their lives with exorbitant tariffs, rampant inflation, vicious nationwide manhunts, and a gratuitous new war? We can’t know, but the results of the midterm election look very much like the beginning of an answer. Related: Voting for the Future of America Donald Trump, the man who would Make America Great Again, is now a lame duck, along with all of the dunces he’s placed in his cabinet and in other positions of power. With control of both houses of Congress soon to pass to the opposition, Trump’s loyal supporters there are about to become as irrelevant as his opponents were until the voters collectively roared “Enough!” and reversed the MAGA tide. The new Congress may even act to rein in the courts, ending their knee-jerk affirmation of Trump’s scofflaw policies and behavior. It looked as if the first of Trump’s dunces to go would be Pete Hegseth, who calls himself Secretary of War, but plainly understands nothing about war. Obsessed with race, gender, and muscular masculinity, Hegseth has rampaged through the senior staff of the most powerful military in the history of the planet, replacing seasoned professionals with successors qualified in his mind because they’re white, male, and motivated by a blind loyalty to their leader. Like the president who appointed him, Hegseth acts as a law unto himself, blustering along from one hair-brained idea to the next, as if he could alter reality by the sheer force of his will. Like others in Trump’s troop of dunces, he’s incapable of imagining he could be wrong. Embarrassing himself almost daily in both word and deed, he “struts and frets his hour upon the stage.” Soon enough he’ll be heard no more, and he’ll be just one more pathetic character in what has become “a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.” It was no surprise, then, that members of the House began impeachment proceedings against him almost as soon as the election results were in. The impeachment vote failed, but once the Republicans have become the minority, their Democratic colleagues can follow through unobstructed. Regardless of what eventually happens to Hegseth and his fellow dunces, the general election of 2028 will determine what their political fate is to be. Related: What I Learned in Nagasaki: We Are Not Innocent When We Look Away If that election continues the trend of the one just ended, Trump’s dunces no longer will be able to ignore the Constitution and the federal statutes, or to replace the rule of law with rule by law, as they try to legislate their brave new world into being. The new Congress will have the opportunity to reverse all of that, and send the dunces back to the shadows they came from after Trump rode down his golden escalator in 2015 and gave them permission to come out of hiding. With a little luck and a lot of effort, a more humane world could come into being, and something like balance could return to American politics. But the luck won’t be enough, without the effort. If we on the side of light can’t or won’t overcome our own differences and work together, not only among ourselves but also with those in the opposition who remain loyal to the ideas of 1776, we’ll just end up as a confederacy of dunces in our own right.

articles.title: Can Xavier Becerra Make Life More Affordable
articles.author: Mark Kreidler
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The affordability issues that drove the midterm elections weren’t mitigated by the mere fact of a blue wave. Democratic leaders in Congress and the individual states still face systemic problems, some of which can appear intractable. That’s especially true in California, where some 14 million residents, more than a third of the population, rely on Medi-Cal, the state’s version of the low-income Medicaid program, for their health care. California’s poverty rate is among the highest in the nation, as it has been for nearly 15 years. The challenge to millions of low-wage workers — find a way to afford life in the Golden State — has never stood taller. But that’s not the same as saying there are no answers. And incoming Democratic governor Xavier Becerra doesn’t need to wait to begin initiating meaningful improvements in the lives of those workers in such critical areas as renter protection, child care and the soaring cost of health care. Interviews with multiple stakeholders and political strategists over the past few weeks have identified a number of actions that Becerra, who will succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom in January, can undertake along with the Democratic supermajority in the state Legislature. Some of those actions directly address affordability issues facing the low-wage workers and their families who form the backbone of many of California’s largest industries. These measures certainly aren’t free. “Meaningfully addressing California’s longstanding affordability crisis will require bold solutions, which in turn will require new state funding,” said Scott Graves, budget director at the California Budget & Policy Center. “To raise revenue, state leaders should focus on ensuring that corporations and the wealthy contribute their fair share of taxes.” That said, here are five ideas that Becerra can begin pursuing almost immediately after taking office: Strengthen renter protections and add forgiveness. California’s Tenant Protection Act puts a cap on how much a landlord can raise the rent each year, but that cap remains onerous: 5% plus a cost of living increase, up to a maximum overall raise of 10%. If a landlord follows that law to the max for even a couple of years in a row, a low-wage worker can quickly be priced out of their own home. Considering California has nearly 16 million renters, that’s an ongoing affordability problem. Lowering the allowable rent increase would be a good first step, along with making the TPA permanent (the law is scheduled to expire in 2030). But there’s something else Becerra and the Legislature can do. Currently, California renters have only three business days after receiving an eviction notice to pay off back rent and remain in their homes. But California could join 21 other “redemption states” in the U.S. that allow a tenant to pay the rent owed and avoid eviction long after such a proceeding is under way — weeks, even. Past efforts to do this have run up against the powerful landlord lobby in Sacramento, so it’s no slam dunk. Related: California's Medi-Cal Crisis Deepens as Billionaire Wealth Tax Falls Short Enforce the labor laws already on the books. “Wage theft takes money straight out of low-wage workers’ pockets,” said Enrique Lopezlira, director of the Low-Wage Work Program at the UC Berkeley Labor Center. “It may be the most direct affordability issue that doesn’t need a new law.” Wage theft, by which employers underpay their workers either intentionally or through payroll mistakes, costs low-wage workers in California at least $2 billion per year , according to the Economic Policy Institute. Other reports suggest the figure could be more than twice that . Once in office, Becerra can redirect resources toward enforcing the state’s wage laws. That includes increasing staffing in the Labor Commissioner’s Office, the better to pursue wage theft claims more aggressively and start collecting past unpaid judgments. Expand access to affordable child care. One of the primary drivers of the affordability crisis for low-wage workers is finding a way to care for their children while they’re on the job — often a crushing, self-defeating expense. Newsom has worked on this issue on and off for years. In 2021, he promised to expand affordable child care by phasing in 200,000 new subsidized spots by 2025-26. He’ll fall far short of that goal , leaving Becerra to pick up the ball and continue running. This is an enormously popular issue; more than three-quarters of Californians surveyed are in favor of increasing state funding so that child care programs are available to more low-wage workers and their families. And Becerra could double down on it by simultaneously pushing for something closer to a living wage for child care workers, whose low reimbursement rates likely contribute to a smaller-than-needed talent pool. Related: California Saves Millions on Home Care: Workers Pay the Price Raise funding to backfill safety-net programs. The Republican-passed H.R. 1 spending bill last year gutted federal Medicaid funding, with California suffering a likely $30 billion per year funding shortfall as a result. Paired with new paperwork requirements for eligible families, it’s going to lead to steep cuts in Medi-Cal enrollment and more California low-wage workers going without health care until they have an emergency. As a candidate, Becerra loudly endorsed proposed “fair share” legislation as one way to offset some of the federal cuts. That law would essentially slap fines on California businesses that pay their employees so little, their workers qualify for Medi-Cal insurance. The fines would be used to help replace the missing federal funds. “Why should we subsidize health care for those folks who are working full time because their employer won’t pay them enough so they can afford health insurance?” Becerra said in August. “If you’re not paying enough for your workers, maybe that means we have to raise taxes on some of these bigger companies.” Strike the new Medi-Cal premiums on immigrants. Under a policy change pushed by Newsom, certain groups of immigrants who use Medi-Cal for their health care will begin paying monthly premiums in 2027. Though the initial figure may be as low as $30 per month, it’s still significant to a low-wage working family that is trying to make ends meet. Becerra and state lawmakers have the authority to either lower or eliminate that premium, likely encouraging more low-wage workers to continue using Medi-Cal. That also potentially reduces costs to hospitals, as patients who can’t afford Medi-Cal are statistically more likely to simply go without coverage, then use the emergency room as a source of care once a condition becomes serious. By law, such care has to be provided by the hospital even if the patient cannot pay. Without question, Becerra also bears a responsibility to work on bigger-picture issues. California’s housing crunch, for example, is by now both generational and the most obvious contributor to the affordability gap facing the state’s low-wage workers. State Speaker of the Assembly Robert Rivas “has boldly led and passed the strongest housing reforms in 20 years,” almost all of it aimed at streamlining the construction process and getting more houses into the pipeline, said Democratic political strategist Steven Maviglio. “Becerra can get on that train and lead with courage, too.” The new governor also will take office at roughly the same time that both houses of Congress come under Democratic control. A number of experts suggested that Becerra and California will need to be at the forefront of working with federal legislators to try to roll back some of H.R. 1’s deepest cuts to safety net programs. But those are long-term projects. California’s low-wage work community needs relief much sooner, not down the line. Becerra and state lawmakers are in a position to start providing just that. Capital & Main

articles.title: DSA SF’s Battle for an Affordable, Equitable San Francisco
articles.author: San Francisco DSA
articles.content: The Democratic Socialists of America won 160 elected offices and ballot measures across the country this month. One of those measures, Proposition B for a San Francisco Public Bank, has been added to the list of DSA SF’s electoral victories. In red states and blue, the message of these midterms was clear: Working people want socialism. However, here at home, our oligarch mayor and his billionaire friends spent record sums to convince San Francisco voters to amend the city charter in order to consolidate control in the Mayor’s Office and limit working class access to the ballot. Socialists, as part of the broader working class movement, went toe to toe with the new San Francisco machine – the coalition of corporate real estate and tech money that has formed around Mayor Lurie – to fight for a San Francisco where everyone can afford to live and thrive, at a time when rents and evictions are rising exponentially without any end or meaningful intervention in sight. Prop I: Affordable Housing Guarantee Act Prop I would have introduced the largest increase in affordable housing production in years, dedicating an average of $120 million each year to housing working families can afford by permanently dedicating revenue from an existing tax on the sale of mansions and skyscrapers to social and affordable housing, rent relief, and eviction defense. Billionaires and corporate landlords spent $2.8 million on a misinformation campaign supported by Mayor Lurie, the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board, and dark money influencers like GrowSF to convince San Franciscans that they should vote against affordable housing. They needed every penny. We mobilized thousands of volunteers, reached 250,000 voters, and earned 48% of the vote against the full might of the machine. While we narrowly lost on election day, Prop I scored a major victory months before the first vote was cast. We brought this measure as a response to Mayor Lurie and Supervisor Bilal Mahmood’s BUILD Act, which proposed to repeal the transfer tax increase that our chapter won at the ballot in 2020. Not only did our pressure contribute to the mayor’s abandonment of that policy in 2026, our campaign momentum forced him into a tacit pledge that transfer tax repeal is off the table. Mayor Lurie dearly wants to give real estate speculators a tax break and call it a housing policy, but now he is on the record saying that doing so would “blow a hole in our city’s budget” taking away “money that could be used for firefighters, public safety, and cleaning our streets.” While the loss of Prop I continues the status quo, it is up to us to hold City Hall accountable to using money collected from Prop I passed in 2020 toward building housing and demand they do so. Through the Prop I campaign, we built bridges with a strong coalition of public sector workers including SEIU 1021 and IFPTE Local 21, the United Educators of San Francisco, tenant organizations, and affordable housing advocates. We knocked doors across buildings in SOMA and the Tenderloin to campaign for Prop I and spread the word about tenants’ rights. Through advocacy, urgent action, and organizing alongside our coalition partners, we will continue to fight for the belief that housing is a human right. We will ensure that publicly-owned social housing is created, and fight the near-constant attempts by real estate speculators and corporate landlords to take over San Francisco. Join this work by coming to an upcoming meeting of our Social Housing or Tenant Organizing working groups. Prop B for a Public Bank The decade-long, DSA SF-led movement for a San Francisco Public Bank scored a historic victory with the passage of Proposition B, which authorizes the functions and governance of the nation’s first municipal public bank. As enabled by Prop B, the San Francisco Public Bank will be a financial institution that prioritizes the public good over private profit to fund the things our city needs most: social and affordable housing, green infrastructure, and local small businesses. And it will do so while keeping our money out of the Wall Street banks which fund climate destruction and imperialism. San Francisco’s Prop B is the first measure of its kind, asking voters to demand a municipal city-owned public bank. The road to Prop B has been a long one: DSA SF’s socialist in office, Supervisor Jackie Fielder, founded the SF Public Bank Coalition in 2017 to establish alternative financing opportunities to achieve maximum local impact. For nearly ten years, the coalition has been driven by working-class people of color deeply embedded in our communities. The grassroots coalition brought together climate justice advocates and community organizers to bring the issue of a public bank to local and regional lawmakers, paving the way to this historic victory. Though it was opposed by corporate interests, dark money groups, and our own Mayor, the coalition was able to beat back misinformation and garner support from a broad coalition of labor and progressive organizations. Alongside the Public Bank Coalition, DSA SF mobilized thousands of volunteers, solicited support from neighborhood groups, and canvassed households across San Francisco to educate and inspire support for a public bank. This win is a lesson in steadfastness—no matter how long it takes, we will continue to fight for the socialist future we all deserve. And it is only through grassroots local organizing efforts that we can win socialist policies like local democratized financing. The passage of Prop B proves San Franciscans are ready to move past traditional capitalist lending strategies that have failed to deliver for our communities. Rather than fill the coffers of Wall Street banks, San Franciscans chose to set an example of community wealth building and the creation of resilient local economies that work for the common good. DSA SF is proud to earn this victory alongside the SF Public Bank Coalition for the people of San Francisco. Join a meeting of our Ecosocialism Working Group to learn about the next steps toward public bank formation and how you can help. Socialists for Schools: Bunny McFadden and Reina Tello We are committed to launching grassroots organizers as candidates. DSA SF also endorsed two longtime grassroots organizers who ran to fight for public education that serves the working class. School board races in San Francisco have long been marred by recalls and PAC-spending. Bunny McFadden and Reina Tello proudly ran as socialists in the City College Board of Trustees and School Board races, respectively. McFadden and Tello were able to garner endorsements from unions, including the United Educators of San Francisco and American Federation of Teachers Local 2121, democratic clubs, and current and former Supervisors from across the City. Both McFadden and Tello ran strong campaigns and never compromised their values. They brought the fight to corporate-backed candidates and ultimately gained the support of working-class families, students, and teachers. We hope their races can build the framework for future grassroots organizers competing for offices like the San Francisco School Board: a post that has historically been used by elites backed by dark money groups to launch the careers of candidates who will carry out the will of corporate interests. Despite these losses, DSA SF is committed to the struggle for public education that supports students and faculty in our city. With rank-and-file members like McFadden and Tello, we know we can continue to build power with students, teachers, and working families to expand public resources like Free City College and win the highest quality public education for our students. No on D, E, F: Opposing the Mayor’s Power Grab We will always fight for the working class to govern, and struggle for a new political system. DSA SF has led grassroots campaigns that triumph at the ballot box, like passing the tenant right to counsel and taxing wealthy real estate speculators to fund affordable housing. This is no doubt why the Mayor’s billionaire allies and astro-turfing groups like GrowSF devoted millions to passing Prop D to limit our democracy. We’ve elected socialist candidates Harry Britt, Dean Preston and Jackie Fielder to the Board of Supervisors to provide critical oversight of the Mayor’s policies and appointees. So, it’s no surprise the Mayor’s allies launched a well-funded misinformation campaign to convince voters that Prop E and Prop F would stop corruption in City Hall—when, in fact, they just centralize power in the Mayor’s office and limit Board oversight. Lurie’s billionaire allies raised over $13.2 million to pass these measures, more than any ballot measure committee in San Francisco history. The success of their power grab absolutely hinders our goal to have working-class people shape City government. It also eliminates any excuses. While his approval rating remains high by some standards, his self-described “moderate” policies mirror the authoritarian, anti-working-class policies of the Republican Party. Conditions for working people have deteriorated on Lurie’s watch: housing costs have skyrocketed thanks to his prioritization of corporate real estate profits. In June, he cut social services, including LGTBQ healthcare and senior care, leaving vacancies across critical departments like Public Health. The Mayor’s massive private PR spending and billionaire alliance can only suspend voters’ disbelief for so long while San Franciscans continue to suffer the consequences of his laissez-faire policies. Across the country, everyday people voted against data centers, mass surveillance, and electeds who support U.S. funding of the ongoing genocide in Palestine — the very things the San Francisco Democratic Party has come to stand for. It’s Up to Us DSA is a fabric of organizers pushing in different lanes toward the same goal: winning socialism. This election is just one small fraction of the continued fight against the entire global system of capital that pits working class people against each other to ensure the rich get richer and stay in power. At its heart, democratic socialism is a movement to provide what all workers want: less of their days spent working and worrying about the bills; healthy homes and families that are cared for; real democratic representation; and a world where we labor for the common good instead of private profit and domination. We push these demands to their furthest extent today, and fight to realize a socialist future tomorrow. The only path forward is to join together with other working San Franciscans committed to winning the world we deserve. If you haven’t yet joined, now is the time to do so. Join us at dsasf.org/join .

articles.title: We Started the School Year with a March on the Principal
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: Our classrooms have been flooding multiple times a year. As demoralized as my co-workers were, this issue had the juice we needed to lead a workplace action — everyone cared enough to do something about it. Photo: Kayla Sharpe By Kayla Sharpe At Ferndale High School, one of our most pressing problems is the dilapidated building, built in the 1950s. The outdated heating and cooling systems are prone to classroom floods — in the last nine months I’ve experienced three. Once boiling hot water sprayed out of the HVAC unit during class, nearly injuring a student. It was late August — our last Sunday night of freedom before our teacher professional development week — when six of my co-workers and I received an email from our principal. She said that a few classrooms had flooded again the previous week, but the damage was limited and our classrooms were “ready for our return.” “Tomorrow is still the beginning of a fresh school year,” she wrote, “and I’m looking forward to welcoming everyone back and starting the year together on a positive note.” She made the mistake of including all affected teachers as recipients, instead of blind copying us, so I knew exactly who to reach out to. That evening I spent lots of time on the phone with my co-workers and my fellow union building representatives. We all had experienced previous flooding, so we were skeptical that our classrooms would actually be ready for our return the following morning. Ever since I began working at this school in 2024, my mission has been to convince my co-workers we should be compensated in some way when our school administrators fail us. Whenever we’ve asked administrators to address issues like poor attendance or facilities problems, we’ve gotten responses like “That is not my fault” or “I do not have the power to fix that.” This energy has been so demoralizing for our teaching staff, and it seemed to me that my co-workers had gotten used to just accepting the b.s. But having cut my teeth as a political organizer on my college campus and read Secrets of a Successful Organizer , I could tell that this issue had the juice we needed to lead a workplace action — everyone cared enough to do something about it. By Monday morning I had devised a plan with the support of my fellow building reps. INDUSTRIAL FANS Our suspicions were correct; words can hardly describe the scene we walked into. Each of the seven flooded classrooms had eight to 15 industrial fans blowing on the floor, dehumidifying machines siphoning water out of the classroom windows, and no functioning air conditioning. Teachers were supposed to spend this day organizing and preparing our classrooms. Most of us spend hundreds of dollars of our own money to purchase supplies, decor, soft lighting, and small comforting touches to make our classrooms the warm, safe environments we know students need. It takes a fair amount of time to unpack those things from the summer months and get the space ready for the school year. When I saw the state of my classroom, I knew it was going to be impossible to get any sort of work done in that environment. My next step was to walk door to door and check in on my six co-workers who had been looped in on that email. No classroom was even close to being a functional workspace. I could feel the swelling anger, and knew the moment was ripe to make an ask. “We do not deserve this,” I told my co-workers. “What if we all went to the principal and asked for something in return?” I told them about the plan the other building reps and I had come up with: The affected teachers could march together to the principal’s office and ask that either we receive pay for the additional hours it takes us to set up our classrooms outside of contract time, or we be excused from a professional development session during the week to set up our classrooms during work hours. Everyone was too angry to be afraid. All but one agreed to join our march on the boss. The six of us found our principal in a teacher’s classroom. She stepped into the hall to see us standing there shoulder to shoulder, looking upset. None of us will ever forget her response: She took out her phone, started filming us, and said, “Oh I am going to put this on TikTok, it’s the first day of school and the teachers already want something from me.” When she saw how deeply stunned we were, she put her phone back in her pocket and asked what was wrong. I reminded her of her email, and informed her that our classrooms were in fact not “ready for our return.” I told her this wasn’t fair to us, and explained how we felt it could be rectified. She said she understood our frustration and would “look into” allowing us to timecard extra hours. We did not feel incredibly hopeful. There’s too much wiggle room in the phrase “I will look into that.” But to our surprise, we received an email from the principal saying she would be able to approve three hours of paid time for classroom setup. LESSONS LEARNED Since this action, I have debriefed with the teachers that participated. While we’re glad we won some compensation, we realized we should have come with a number in mind. We were doubtful that we would win any kind of concession, so we didn’t even think that far ahead. We were able to get the most necessary work done within the three approved hours, but could have benefited from more time. Still, once the rest of our staff heard about our action, our building was buzzing with excitement. I heard co-workers 15 to 25 years my senior say, “That was so cool!” “I didn’t even know you could do that!” “I wish I was as brave as you when I was your age!” So in my mind, it was a success. I think the most powerful thing we can do as organizers is be hopeful, and share that hope. The message of “You do not deserve this mistreatment” seemed to really resonate. In education, we grow so used to getting beat down from all angles that we can forget we deserve to be treated with dignity. I’m very proud to have helped my co-workers work together at that moment. I hope this will help us find the courage to take on our next workplace issue without fear. Kayla Sharpe is a high school social studies teacher in Ferndale, Michigan, and a building representative with the Ferndale Education Association. We Started the School Year with a March on the Principal was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Transgender Day of Remembrance — Why We Fight
articles.author: DSA National Statements
articles.content: [Content Warning – Violence and Suicide] This year, over 50* Transgender Americans have lost their lives due to societal violence. One of these is 29 year old Hailey Singleton from Dunnellon, who while living in Florida, was found along a dirt road with gunshot wounds. Davonta Curtis from Chicago, Illinois is one of the many BIPOC Trans people that are no longer with us. In Boise, Idaho, May Pollard is one of the three youngest people listed at 16 years old. She, along with Sydney Lou Walden from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, were one of at least 20 who committed suicide. On November 20th, crowds across the country are gathering for Transgender Day of Remembrance, where poets, priests and local politicians will speak about the plight of America’s (arguably) most marginalized and targeted minority for demonization by the American political establishment. Members of the community will talk about friends, family, brothers, sisters and siblings that have been lost to a society that has refused to accept them. Parents will mourn their children. Children will mourn their parents. The names of the dead will be remembered, and the community that rallies around them will collectively answer the question of why we fight — the names of those lost. In 2017, DSA’s Queer Socialist Working Group, now known as the Queer and Feminist Commission, argued that Trans people are scapegoated by conservatives as part of the barbaric process of creating the inequality that capitalism feeds on. Nine years later, we ask another question: How will we fight back against that barbarism? Our existence in society has been challenged at a fundamental level. Hostile investigations are launched, oftentimes victimizing gender non-conforming cis-women, when someone suspects a Transgender person has “Invaded” the “wrong bathroom”, demanding that the accused expose their body to satisfy investigators. After moving from Iowa to Minnesota, which has passed trans refuge laws, two Trans Minnesotans were attacked in public, with onlookers cheering on the assault. In this country, after being pushed to the ground during an onslaught of bigoted language, if one of us draws a weapon in clear self defense, we face felony charges and have our fundraiser campaigns for medical expenses suspended thanks to GoFundMe. Protections for Trans people against sexual abuse in prisons and ICE detentions centers have been eliminated . Gender identity is no longer a protected class to protect from discrimination in Iowa. Many of us are prohibited from updating our documentation to have the correct name and gender. In Kansas, chances are your documents were made invalid before you even had the opportunity to update them. It’s clear that this government has targeted us. Anyone who demeans our existence and regurgitates bigotry in the name of electability are not our allies. When they demand that we engage in the politics of assimilation and respectability, they are not our allies. Indiana’s soon to be Secretary of State Beau Bayh and Ohio’s soon-to-be Governor Amy Acton were two of many candidates that regurgitated anti-trans rhetoric by agreeing with statements like “we should not have men playing women’s sports,” suggesting they view Trans women as men. In Washington, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won reelection handedly even after voting for a bill to out Trans students to parents. Josh Turek, the newly elected Democratic US Senator from Iowa, released an ad in the last few days of the election cycle to advocate for the ending of all federal funding for gender affirming care, which is a stance more harmful and transphobic than the Republican party has yet to suggest. With Democrats like these, who needs Republicans? Hostility towards Trans people has gained ground. At the same time, efforts to defend, support, and uplift the Trans community have only gotten stronger. To start, the anti-trans ballot measure in Missouri , which was linked to a potential abortion ban, was rejected by voters by an almost eleven point margin. And while the country was celebrating an electoral victory against our fascist government and its illegal wars, the Transgender community was rallying and protesting in the state capitols where the ballot measures were successful, like Arizona and Colorado, as they sought to undermine our right to exist. The fight against these ballot measures and for our dignity has been taken to court, with parents of transgender and cisgender students joining legal efforts to block the anti-trans sports ballot measure in Washington from going into effect. We’ve seen victories for trans rights in Virginia, New York and Seattle, as America’s Presidential administration walks back a rule that would have withheld federal funds for hospitals that provide gender affirming care for Trans youth. The midterms have seen a number of accomplices within the political establishment elected. Victoria Broderick, the US House Rep-elect from the fourth Congressional district in Tennessee come January specifically called out candidates speaking about Trans people in sports, saying that “any politician talking about men in women’s sports is a lazy politician.” US Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed from Michigan, has been a strong ally of trans rights. When pressed on the issue by Bari Weiss’ 60 Minutes he stated “I believe in rights. And even though somebody might use rights that you don’t understand, you never mean to use yourself, you still have to show up and fight for those rights.” What’s even more encouraging are the Democratic Socialists elected this cycle that are unapologetic and unfiltered with their support for Trans people. Such examples include Claire Valdez from New York City, who had a section on her policy page entitled “Queer and Trans Liberation,” and Melat Kiros from Denver, who displayed a “TRANS BILL OF RIGHTS” on hers. In the halls of power where our bodies have been legislated upon, our voices have been added to the conversation. From the South in Florida and Georgia, to the Midwest in Michigan, a sentiment starts to become unignorable: Your comfort does not justify silencing us, and we will not be silent in the face of bigotry against us. Jaelynn Scott, the second Democratic Socialist elected to Washington’s state legislature, the first Trans woman elected to Washington’s state legislature, and the first openly Trans Black woman elected to public office, had this to say about what these electoral victories meant. “Not only can we lead, but we can lead with power, with your brilliance, and our principles. We can lead proudly, as Black Trans women, as Trans women, as Trans men, as Non-Binary people, we can be ourselves. Let this win represent that to you and know that you can go as far as you want to. I got your back, and this community has your back.” We were not the first scapegoat for their barbarism, and we will not be the last. Only through a solidarity that unites all working people against this exploitative system can we be free. With recognition that the capitalist system must have a scapegoat, none of us are free until we are all free — until we reject the inherent bigotry of this system. Dear siblings — Get out and organize. If you can see these oppressions as linked, stand with the DSA to fight against all forms of inequality. A better world is possible, and Trans people will be liberated in that world. DSA Queer Feminist Commission and Trans Rights and Bodily Autonomy Campaign DSA National Political Committee *While many organizations may be referring to the number of Trans people that were victims of violence, we decided to use the number provided by Remembering Our Dead to account for the social, political, or economic systems that contribute to the premature death of Trans people. Even then, the number is likely higher than the one accounted for. The post Transgender Day of Remembrance — Why We Fight appeared first on Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) .

articles.title: Amazon Is Ratcheting Up Its Fight With NYC Delivery Drivers
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content: New Yorkers opening Amazon’s app on Thursday were greeted with a warning: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” A link invited them to “act now to protect low prices,” directing customers to contact their city council members about legislation that would require Amazon to directly employ its delivery drivers. Amazon rolled out the warnings, which also appear on packages delivered in the New York area, as part of its campaign against New York City’s Delivery Protection Act (DPA), which an Amazon-funded coalition has already spent upward of $8 million opposing. Amazon is warning customers that the legislation would put small delivery companies out of business, eliminate jobs, and delay their packages. The company has not explained how it calculated the additional $5 per order. The act’s partisans say Amazon’s threats are absurd. “The Delivery Protection Act would require companies like Amazon to pay a $500 licensing fee every other year and comply with workplace and public safety regulations,” Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s lead sponsor, told Jacobin . “It’s simply dishonest to claim that this bill would require them to charge consumers $5 for every delivery. New Yorkers won’t let themselves be bullied by corporations and billionaires.” “It’s a slap in the face to hardworking people everywhere,” Tony Rosario, a New York–based organizer for the Teamsters Amazon Division, told me. “You have to have some nerve to try to blame the city council for holding Amazon accountable.” He dismissed the company’s threats to leave the city should the legislation pass. “They’re not leaving New York City,” he said. The city is largely thought to be the company’s biggest market in the country. Mayor Zohran Mamdani also responded to the warnings Thursday afternoon. “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council’s efforts to protect workers’ rights and keep our streets safe,” he tweeted . “It’s greed.” Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash similarly used their apps to campaign for California’s Proposition 22 in 2020, spending more than $200 million to pass a measure allowing them to continue treating drivers as independent contractors. The legislation Amazon is fighting in New York would change who employs its sprawling delivery-driver workforce. Cabán’s bill would require operators of last-mile delivery facilities to employ their drivers and warehouse workers directly. Amazon currently contracts out much of that work to smaller companies known as Delivery Service Partners (DSPs). The bill would also impose licensing, safety, and training requirements on delivery facilities, with protections for workers whose jobs are affected by the change. Thirty-four of the fifty-one City Council members have signed on as sponsors, and Mayor Mamdani supports the bill. Council Speaker Julie Menin, however, has yet to bring it to a vote. Councilmembers are negotiating changes to the legislation, including whether to retain the ban on subcontracting, which Amazon is particularly determined to defeat. When the company began planning its own delivery network in 2013, executives worried that entering the transportation business would expose it to organized labor. “A primary concern was whether getting into the transportation business would expose them to unions,” executives involved in those discussions told journalist Brad Stone. When Amazon launched the DSP program several years later, it could run its own delivery network while leaving the drivers on someone else’s payroll. The Teamsters have spent years fighting to establish that Amazon is a joint employer of those drivers and therefore has to bargain with their union. Amazon has threatened to challenge the DPA in court, and the bill is now fueling a steady stream of criticism in the right-wing New York Post . But the legislation could still pass without the requirement that Amazon directly employ its drivers. The current version of the bill would spare workers years of litigation at the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to establish that Amazon is their employer and therefore must bargain with their union. That wouldn’t guarantee a collective bargaining agreement, but it would eliminate one of the company’s principal defenses against unionization. Amazon has funded its multimillion-dollar lobbying and advertising campaign through the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, which operates publicly as New York Delivers. Its advertisements feature DSP owners and drivers warning that the legislation would eliminate small businesses and raise prices. Amazon says that more than forty DSPs in New York City employ over five thousand workers whose jobs could be threatened if the companies were prohibited from contracting with Amazon. The company has also raised the possibility of moving delivery facilities outside city limits. The Teamsters’ Rosario said the concern is misplaced — and that the bill could help DSP owners too. “They’re being squeezed just as much as their employees are,” he said. DSP owners are responsible for maintaining and repairing vehicles and bear much of the responsibility when drivers are injured or involved in accidents. Under the existing arrangement, Rosario said, DSPs serve as a “scapegoat” for the company. Opposition to the bill includes the city’s chambers of commerce and the National Urban League, which has argued that the legislation would particularly harm black-owned delivery businesses. Amazon is listed among the organization’s highest-tier corporate donors, a category representing contributions of at least $1 million. On November 16, the National Urban League and the Amazon-backed New York Delivers coalition threatened legal action if the bill passes in its current form. Their attorney argued that the legislation conflicts with federal and state law. An earlier memo prepared by Brendan McGuire, an attorney at WilmerHale retained by the Amazon-funded Five Borough Jobs Campaign, argued that the bill could violate federal restrictions on local regulation of motor carriers. Menin, who supported an earlier version of the bill, has held off on backing the current one. She has raised concerns about potential job losses, higher prices for consumers, and whether the legislation would survive a legal challenge. A spokesman for the Mamdani administration’s Law Department told The New York Times that he was confident the final legislation would withstand legal scrutiny. The Times also reported that Menin has considered a version of the bill that would license and regulate delivery warehouses without requiring Amazon to directly employ its drivers, though she has not ruled out retaining the subcontracting ban. The New York Post reports that councilmembers are considering requiring warehouse operators to own the delivery vehicles currently owned or leased by contractors. Other details are still being negotiated, including how large a warehouse must be to fall under the law. Sources familiar with the negotiations expect the text to be finalized next week. “Direct employment is one of the most important provisions of the bill,” Rosario said. He said there had been some discussion of exceptions for truly independent contractors but was adamant that Amazon shouldn’t be exempt from the direct-employment requirement. “There’s no way they’re getting around that language,” he said. Menin has insisted that the council will regulate Amazon while protecting jobs and consumer prices. On Thursday, she criticized the company’s new direct appeals to customers. “It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote on X. “We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.” “If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong,” she added. The Teamsters called Amazon’s warnings to customers “extortion by one of the richest corporations in human history” and accused the company of caring about neither its workers nor its customers. The legislation has attracted support from across New York City’s labor movement, including the Central Labor Council, the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union, the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, and the New York Taxi Workers Alliance. On October 22, hundreds of Amazon workers and Teamsters rallied outside city hall, joined by representatives of other unions, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Teamsters President Sean O’Brien. O’Brien accused Menin of failing to keep her promise to bring the bill to a vote. “Keep your promises; don’t fall in love with corporate America,” O’Brien said. “Speaker Menin, you need to do what the people want — the people that put you where you’re at.” The campaign has extended well beyond the rally, with New York City Democratic Socialists of America (NYC-DSA) playing a central role alongside Teamsters Local 804. NYC-DSA has put its electoral canvassing operation to work on the bill, organizing phone banks and sending volunteers door-to-door. By October, they had knocked on more than 11,000 doors and helped bring three councilmembers on as sponsors. In Menin’s Upper East Side district alone, more than 100 volunteers knocked on 2,500 doors in a single day. Mamdani has continued campaigning for the legislation, too. At the October rally, he pointed to the contradiction at the center of Amazon’s employment arrangements. “When a driver wears an Amazon vest, drives an Amazon van, [and] follows a route Amazon set and Amazon insists that driver does not work for them, what is that if not exploitation?” he said. When reporters asked Mamdani about the possibility of dropping the ban on subcontracting and passing a narrower bill, he rejected the idea. “I don’t think that we need to have a conversation about a new bill,” he said. “I think we have all of the answers in the bill as it currently stands.” When I spoke with Julie Su, Mamdani’s deputy mayor for economic justice and the former acting US secretary of labor, about the bill earlier this year, she described Amazon’s arrangement as “a business model built on getting all the benefits of labor while disclaiming any responsibility for it.” “It is an end run around a century of labor protections that have been fought for and won,” she said. Su also took issue with Amazon’s warnings that the bill would cost workers their jobs. “It is an age-old argument by corporations who have profited massively off the backs of exploited workers, to say that working people only have two choices: a really bad job in which you’re struggling to get by, or no job at all,” she told me. “We reject that as a false choice.” Amazon has itself put drivers out of work by cutting ties with DSPs whose employees unionized. Last year in Queens, 105 drivers at Cornucopia Logistics lost their jobs when Amazon canceled its contract with the company. The drivers had organized with the Teamsters and accused Amazon of retaliating against them. Amazon denied it. In Palmdale, California, Amazon cut ties with Battle-Tested Strategies, a contractor whose eighty-four drivers had organized with the Teamsters in 2023. The NLRB later accused Amazon of illegally ending the contract and refusing to bargain. Drivers at another Amazon contractor in Skokie, Illinois, struck in 2024, alleging retaliation for organizing. Amazon denied retaliating against union supporters. The DSP arrangement has also cost New York workers jobs when union organizing wasn’t involved. Last week, the company terminated its relationship with Kaizen Management Solutions, a Manhattan contractor whose employees deliver Amazon packages on electric cargo bikes. Roughly two hundred workers learned that their employment would end November 18. Amazon said it had discovered safety violations and fraud involving the recording of drivers’ hours; some workers disputed that explanation. “This DSP model is about Amazon’s bottom line,” one worker told Streetsblog . “The model that allegedly creates jobs just laid off 200 people right before the holidays.” “I wish I could tell you I have another thing lined up but I don’t,” he added. “They didn’t even give me a month to figure it out.” Rosario met Kaizen’s owner, Ezra Tilaye, at a Teamsters picket outside the Delancey Street facility earlier this week. Tilaye, who is from Guyana, seemed as blindsided by Amazon’s decision as the workers. One driver Rosario spoke with had been on the job for only three days; another had just been promoted to dispatcher. Rosario took that as evidence that Tilaye hadn’t known the contract was about to be terminated. For Rosario, the layoffs made a mockery of Amazon’s campaign to defend small businesses, particularly those owned by minorities. “Are you protecting small businesses, or do you just not care and are pretending otherwise?” he asked. Menin called the layoffs “terrible” and said that the city would regulate Amazon “in a very significant way.” Amazon may not need to defeat the bill outright. The majority of councilmembers have signed on, but negotiations could still strip out the requirement that Amazon employ its drivers directly. Similar legislation has already been introduced in Chicago , and worker advocates want to pursue it in other cities. What survives the negotiations in New York could shape those efforts elsewhere. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
